reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: True umbilical hernias in infants protrude through the umbilical ring and most close spontaneously within the first few years of life
In adults the defect is usually paraumbilical, occurring through the linea alba just above or below the umbilicus, and does not resolve without surgery
Adult paraumbilical hernias are more frequent in women, and predisposing factors include obesity, multiparity, ascites, and chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure
The neck is often narrow relative to the sac, so incarceration and strangulation are relatively common, particularly with a fibrous fatty omental content
Contents may include omentum, small bowel, or transverse colon, and long-standing hernias can become multiloculated
Elective repair (suture repair for small defects, mesh for larger ones) is advised for symptomatic or enlarging adult hernias to avoid emergency complications
In children, repair is usually deferred and reserved for defects that persist beyond a few years, are large, or become complicated
Skin changes over a large tense hernia, such as thinning or ulceration, warrant urgent assessment
reference.pathophysiology: Umbilical and paraumbilical hernias arise from a defect at or adjacent to the umbilical cicatrix. In infants the umbilical ring fails to close fully after cord separation. In adults, weakening and separation of the linea alba fibres around the umbilicus, combined with sustained raised intra-abdominal pressure from obesity, pregnancy, or ascites, allows protrusion of preperitoneal fat, omentum, or bowel through a paraumbilical defect. The characteristically narrow, fibrous neck restricts reduction and readily compromises the vascular supply of trapped contents, predisposing to incarceration and strangulation.
additionalDifferentials: Umbilical granuloma or omphalitis in infants
Metastatic umbilical nodule (Sister Mary Joseph nodule)
Lipoma or sebaceous cyst of the umbilicus
additionalInvestigations: Clinical examination for reducibility, cough impulse, and defect size
Ultrasound to confirm the defect and characterise contents when uncertain
CT in large, recurrent, or complex hernias and to assess in patients with ascites
Assessment for underlying causes of raised intra-abdominal pressure such as ascites
redFlags: Irreducible, tense, tender umbilical swelling indicating incarceration or strangulation (surgical emergency)
Features of bowel obstruction with an irreducible hernia
Overlying skin ischaemia, ulceration, or impending rupture over a large hernia
Systemic sepsis or peritonism suggesting strangulated bowel
reference.prognosis: Most infantile umbilical hernias close spontaneously. Adult paraumbilical hernias do not resolve and carry a meaningful risk of incarceration and strangulation; elective mesh repair gives good results, whereas emergency surgery, especially in obese or comorbid patients, is associated with higher complication rates.
pitfalls: Assuming an adult paraumbilical hernia will behave like a self-resolving infantile hernia
Underestimating strangulation risk because of the narrow neck
Overlooking uncontrolled ascites, which increases recurrence and complicates repair
Missing a Sister Mary Joseph nodule by attributing all umbilical lumps to hernia
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Conservative observation of infantile umbilical hernias, most of which close spontaneously through the umbilical ring in the first few years
Elective surgical repair for adult paraumbilical hernias, which do not resolve, using suture repair for small defects and mesh for larger ones
Addressing contributory causes of raised intra-abdominal pressure such as obesity and ascites to reduce recurrence risk
Emergency surgical repair for incarceration or strangulation, given the narrow neck and risk of compromise to trapped omentum or bowel
Prompt escalation and surgical referral for an irreducible, painful or tender hernia suggesting strangulation
